title: Kabir: one light made all
hook: first came the light, and all creation from it, so who is good and who is bad (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1349)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir the weaver. Your line was the loom is the prayer. Did one piece of ordinary work feel a little like prayer? Today, one of Kabir's most loved verses, sung in gurdwaras around the world. Day two hundred fifty-four.
screen: `KABIR THE WEAVER — THE LOOM IS THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Light a single candle in a dark room. Now light a second candle from it, and a third from that, and a hundred more down a long hall. Which flame is the real one? Which is higher-born? It's a silly question. They're all the first flame, passed along. Kabir lived in a city split by labels: Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, pure and impure. People fought over which flame was the real one. Kabir answered with a verse the Gurus placed in the Granth. Today, Kabir: one light made all.
screen: `ONE CANDLE LIGHTS A HUNDRED.` → `WHICH FLAME IS HIGHER?` → `A CITY SPLIT BY LABELS.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1349, in Rag Prabhati, Kabir sings: awal allah noor upaaiaa kudrat ke sabh bande; ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa kaun bhale ko mande. First, God created the light; all people are creatures of that creation. From one light the whole world welled up; so who is good, and who is bad? Look at the words he chose. Allah, the Arabic name for God. Noor, the Arabic and Persian word for light. Kudrat, creation, nature. A Muslim-born weaver, singing in words his Muslim neighbors would know, to a city full of Hindus too, and saying the same thing to both: you came from the same light. The next lines, in paraphrase: people, don't wander in doubt. The Creator is in the creation, and the creation is in the Creator, filling every place. It's worth hearing why this landed so hard in Kabir's day. He's not saying everyone's the same, or that differences don't exist. He's saying the labels were never the source. Before the temple and the mosque, before castes and clans, there was one light, and everyone is lit from it. And the question at the end is real: who is good, who is bad? Not as a shrug about right and wrong, but as a warning about sorting people by birth. The Sikh Gurus sang the same thing in their own words, which is why this verse sits comfortably in their book. And it's why Sikhs so often quote it when strangers need to become neighbors.
screen: `AWAL ALLAH NOOR — FIRST, THE LIGHT.` · `EK NOOR — ONE LIGHT, ONE WORLD.` · `THE SAME WORDS FOR TWO NEIGHBORS.` · `WHO IS GOOD, WHO IS BAD?` · then, large: `FROM ONE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a stranger you passed recently: on the train, in a store, on a screen. Hold their face in mind. Now picture a small flame in them, lit from the same first light as yours. Not a sentiment; just see it. Try it with one more stranger, then one more. Let the breath slow. If it helps, say it quietly on the out-breath: from one light. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. Here, his verse in Prabhati: from one light the whole world came, so who is good and who is bad by birth?
Your line: from one light. Today, look at one stranger as family, lit from the same flame. Day two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Kabir's verse awal allah noor upaaiaa is widely sung as a shabad in Sikh kirtan and is often quoted by Sikhs to speak of the oneness of humanity.

fork.reveal: ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa: every label comes after the one light.

original.note: Gurmukhi: noor, light; an Arabic and Persian word that Kabir uses for the first light of creation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about everyone being equal.
what it means: all people came from one divine light, so birth labels can't make anyone good or bad.
what a scholar hears: Prabhati Kabir, Ang 1349; awal, noor and kudrat are Perso-Arabic words, and the next line (khaalik khalak, khalak meh khaalik) echoes Sufi language of the Creator in creation.
